summary: This document specifies DHCPv6, an extensible way to configure nodes with network parameters, IPv6 addresses and prefixes. Parameters can be given statelessly or together with stateful assignment of addresses and prefixes. It is an Internet Standard and obsoletes RFC 8415.

eli5.summary: When a computer joins a network, it asks a helper for an address and settings. DHCPv6 is how that helper answers on IPv6.

questions: what udp ports does dhcpv6 use
subtitle: How an IPv6 device asks a server for addresses, delegated prefixes and other network settings.

tldr.problem: IPv6 devices often need more than self-made addresses: managed addresses, delegated prefixes, and settings such as DNS and NTP server lists, handed out by a central server.
tldr.mechanism: DHCPv6 is a client/server protocol over UDP. A client multicasts a Solicit to find servers, picks one, and leases addresses or prefixes through options, with relay agents carrying messages across links.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9915 is the current Internet Standard for DHCPv6. It obsoletes RFC 8415, applies errata, and obsoletes the IA_TA option, the Server Unicast option and the UseMulticast status code.

today: RFC 9915 is an Internet Standard and has not been obsoleted. It obsoletes RFC 8415, so it is the current DHCPv6 specification.

sections.title: What DHCPv6 Does
sections.content:
DHCPv6 is a client/server protocol that provides managed configuration of devices. Basic operation serves clients on the same link as the server, and relay agents let clients and servers on different links talk. A server can give a device addresses plus other configuration, all carried in options, and new options can be defined to extend the protocol.

DHCPv6 also supports automated prefix delegation, where a server hands whole IPv6 prefixes to clients. The RFC notes that other documents call these roles requesting router and delegating router. A client that wants only settings, with no addresses or prefixes, can use stateless DHCPv6, which needs no server-side state and is much simpler than the stateful mode.

This document obsoletes RFC 8415. It applies verified errata and obsoletes two features that were not widely implemented: temporary addresses via the IA_TA option, and clients unicasting messages to a server that sent the Server Unicast option. It also clarifies the UDP ports. Server policy, server management and merging DHCPv4 with DHCPv6 are out of scope.
sections.eli5: DHCPv6 is a helpful office clerk for a network. You ask the clerk for a desk number and some office rules, and the clerk gives them to you.

sections.title: The Message Exchanges
sections.content:
Clients and servers exchange DHCP messages over UDP. A client uses a link-local source address and sends every message to the reserved link-scoped multicast address ff02::1:2 (All_DHCP_Relay_Agents_and_Servers), so it needs no configured server address. A relay agent on the client's link forwards messages to servers elsewhere, and this is transparent to the client.

To get addresses or prefixes, a client normally uses four messages. It sends Solicit to find servers, any suitable server answers with Advertise, the client picks one and sends Request, and the server returns a Reply with the leases and configuration. Clients that only want settings use a two-message Information-request and Reply exchange.

A client may ask for a faster two-message Solicit and Reply exchange by including the Rapid Commit option. Servers may or may not honor it. Each address or prefix has preferred and valid lifetimes. The client sends Renew to extend them, and if a server cannot extend, it returns the address or prefix with lifetimes of 0. A server can also send Reconfigure to tell a client to refresh its configuration.
sections.eli5: The computer calls out to everyone, 'Who can help?' Helpers wave back, it picks one, asks for what it needs and gets it. Later it checks in to keep it longer, and says goodbye when done.

sections.title: Operational Models
sections.content:
The RFC describes the common ways DHCPv6 is used, and they can be combined. A device may start stateful to get an address and later use stateless mode to request more parameters.

  • Stateless DHCP is the simplest mode. Client and server support only Information-request and Reply, plus Relay-forward and Relay-reply when relays are involved.
  • Non-temporary address assignment was the original motivation. It suits cases where stateless address autoconfiguration alone is insufficient, for example because of network policy or dynamic DNS updates.
  • Prefix delegation lets, for example, an ISP delegate a prefix to a subscriber's router. In the RFC's example the client subnets a delegated /48 prefix into /64 prefixes, one for each link in the subscriber network.
  • Customer edge routers combine address assignment and prefix delegation in a single set of transactions.

Addresses derived from a delegated prefix MUST NOT have lifetimes longer than the prefix's remaining lifetimes. A client that has delegated any of the space MUST NOT release the delegated prefix while any of it is outstanding. The RFC also points to RFC 9686 for a way to register self-generated addresses with a server.
sections.eli5: Some people only ask the clerk for the rules. Some ask for a desk. An internet company can give a whole floor to a customer, and the customer then splits it into rooms.

sections.title: Message and Option Formats
sections.content:
All client and server messages share a fixed header followed by a variable options area. The header has a 1-octet msg-type and a 3-octet transaction-id, which lets clients and servers match replies to requests. A client SHOULD pick a random, hard-to-guess transaction ID and MUST leave it unchanged in retransmissions. All values are in network byte order and options are stored one after another with no padding.

Relay agents use a different header shared by Relay-forward and Relay-reply: msg-type (12 or 13), a 1-octet hop-count, a 16-octet link-address that helps the server identify the client's link, and a 16-octet peer-address holding the address of the client or relay that sent the relayed message. The original message travels inside a Relay Message option.

Every option has a 2-octet option-code, a 2-octet option-len and the option data. Options can nest. For example, the IA_NA option contains IA Address options. Unknown options MUST be ignored rather than causing a message to be discarded, which the RFC calls critical for future extensions. Domain names are encoded as in RFC 1035 section 3.1 and name compression MUST NOT be used.
sections.eli5: Every message is an envelope with a short label on the front (what kind it is and a ticket number) and then a stack of notes inside. Notes the helper does not understand are just skipped.

sections.title: DUIDs and Identity Associations
sections.content:
Each client and server has exactly one DUID (DHCP Unique Identifier). It is a 2-octet type code followed by an identifier of 1 to 128 octets. Four types are defined: link-layer address plus time (1), vendor-assigned based on an Enterprise Number (2), link-layer address (3) and UUID (4). Clients and servers MUST treat a DUID as opaque and only compare it for equality, and it SHOULD NOT change over time if at all possible.

An Identity Association (IA) groups a set of related addresses or delegated prefixes, and each IA has a client-chosen IAID. The IAID MUST be unique among the client's IAs of that type and consistent across client restarts. IA_NA carries non-temporary addresses and IA_PD carries delegated prefixes. An IA_NA belongs to exactly one interface, while an IA_PD need not.

The server keeps a binding indexed by DUID, IA type and IAID. Each IA carries the timers T1 (when to ask the original server to renew) and T2 (when to ask any server to rebind). Lifetimes and timers are unsigned 32-bit values in seconds, and 0xffffffff means infinity.
sections.eli5: The DUID is a name tag that never changes. An identity association is a labelled bag where the helper writes down which things it lent you. T1 and T2 are alarm clocks that tell you when to ask for more time.

sections.title: Reliability and Retransmission
sections.content:
Messages travel over UDP, so the client is responsible for reliable delivery. If it gets no expected response, it retransmits with an exponential backoff and a random factor RAND between -0.1 and +0.1, which keeps many clients from synchronizing. A retransmission updates the Elapsed Time option. The first timeout is based on the initial time (IRT), each later one roughly doubles, and a maximum (MRT), retry count (MRC) or duration (MRD) can stop the exchange.

Table 1 of the RFC gives the defaults. Examples are SOL_TIMEOUT of 1 second, SOL_MAX_RT of 3600 seconds, REQ_MAX_RC of 10 attempts, REN_TIMEOUT of 10 seconds, and a HOP_COUNT_LIMIT of 8.

A client MUST also limit how fast it sends DHCP messages, enforced per interface. A token bucket is recommended and a possible default is 20 messages in 20 seconds. When T1 or T2 is 0, the client picks its own renew and rebind times, MUST NOT transmit immediately, and MUST respect the rate limit. The client SHOULD delay its first Solicit by a random time between 0 and SOL_MAX_DELAY (1 second) to desynchronize clients after, for example, a power failure.
sections.eli5: If nobody answers, you knock again, waiting a bit longer each time and a random little extra, so a hallway of kids does not all knock at once. You also should not knock a hundred times a second.

sections.title: Key Options and Status Codes
sections.content:
Section 21 defines the base options. The most important are OPTION_CLIENTID (1) and OPTION_SERVERID (2), which carry DUIDs, OPTION_IA_NA (3) and OPTION_IAADDR (5) for addresses, OPTION_ORO (6), the Option Request option the client uses to list options it wants, OPTION_PREFERENCE (7), OPTION_ELAPSED_TIME (8), OPTION_RELAY_MSG (9), OPTION_AUTH (11), OPTION_STATUS_CODE (13), OPTION_RAPID_COMMIT (14), OPTION_IA_PD (25) and OPTION_IAPREFIX (26). Others cover vendor data, interface IDs, reconfigure support and refresh times.

The Status Code option reports success or failure. If it is absent, the status is assumed to be Success. When choosing among Advertise messages, a client SHOULD prefer the highest server preference value, but MAY choose a less preferred server that offers a better set of parameters.

The obsoleted pieces are the IA_TA option (code 4), the Server Unicast option (code 12) and the UseMulticast status code (5). IANA has marked them Obsolete in its registries.
sections.eli5: Options are the little sticky notes in the envelope: 'here is my name', 'please give me an address', 'here is the answer', 'everything went fine' or 'sorry, none left'.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC treats the DHCP threat as inherently an insider threat. DHCP lacks end-to-end encryption between clients and servers, so hijacking, tampering and eavesdropping are all possible. Both sides face resource-exhaustion denial of service, which servers can partly mitigate by limiting leases per client, declines and message rates.

A malicious server can hand clients wrong configuration, such as incorrect DNS or NTP servers, or set unreasonably high SOL_MAX_RT and INF_MAX_RT values. Servers face invalid clients that masquerade as valid ones. Relay-to-server messages can be protected with IPsec, as described in RFC 8213, though manually configured pre-shared keys do not defend against replay.

For Reconfigure messages the RFC defines the Reconfiguration Key Authentication Protocol (RKAP). The server sends a key in the first exchange and later signs Reconfigure messages, and a client MUST discard any Reconfigure that is unauthenticated or fails validation. The key itself can be compromised if the first exchange is intercepted. On privacy, the RFC refers readers to RFC 7824 for identifiers that could track a client and to RFC 7844 for mitigations.
sections.eli5: Anyone in the room could pretend to be the helper or listen in. So there are rules to slow down troublemakers, and a secret handshake so a computer only believes 'please ask again' notes from its real helper.

messages.label: Renew
messages.note: Sent when the T1 timer expires.

messages.label: Reply
messages.note: Server discards the lease or leases.

items.label: REQUEST
items.desc: Client requests configuration from a specific server.

items.label: CONFIRM
items.desc: Client checks its addresses are still appropriate to the link.

items.label: RENEW
items.desc: Client extends leases with the original server.

items.label: REBIND
items.desc: Client extends leases with any server.

items.label: REPLY
items.desc: Server answers with leases and configuration.

items.label: DECLINE
items.desc: Client reports an address already in use.

items.label: INFORMATION-REQUEST
items.desc: Client asks for parameters without leases.

items.label: RELAY-REPL
items.desc: Server replies through a relay agent.

fields.name: transaction-id
fields.desc: Matches responses to the exchange. A 3-octet field.

fields.name: hop-count
fields.desc: Number of relay agents that have already relayed this message.

fields.name: link-address
fields.desc: Lets the server identify the link the client is on.

fields.name: peer-address
fields.desc: Address of the client or relay agent the relayed message came from.

data.title: Computing RT
data.code:
RT = IRT + RAND*IRT

RT = 2*RTprev + RAND*RTprev

if (RT > MRT)
   RT = MRT + RAND*MRT
